findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type
findings.body: In Service.Check the denial key is built from namespace, UserUID, action, name and parent folder, but not IdentityType. Different subject types can yield the same UserUID (for example user:test-uid vs service-account:test-uid, or anonymous:0 vs render:0). A denial cached for one identity type will then cause Check for a different identity type with the same UID string to return Allowed:false without consulting the database. This is an authorization correctness bug that can deny legitimate access across user, service-account, anonymous and render identities.

findings.title: Denial cache creates stale-deny window blocking DB fallback
findings.body: Check returns immediately on permDenialCache hit and only falls back to getIdentityPermissions from the DB when there is no denial entry. A denial is then cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) whenever the DB path denies. If permissions are granted after a deny, or the DB read lagged behind the write (replica lag, or Check raced the permission commit), every retry within the TTL hits the denial cache and never re-queries the DB. This reintroduces the staleness the PR claims to fix and can lock out a dashboard/folder creator for up to the TTL after an initial premature deny.

findings.title: DB fallback still uses stale team, role and folder caches
findings.body: The new Check fallback calls getIdentityPermissions to get fresh permissions, but getUserPermissions reuses getUserBasicRole, getUserTeams and buildFolderTree, all of which are themselves cached for shortCacheTTL. A new grant via team membership, basic-role change, or a new folder hierarchy therefore still resolves with stale teams/roles/tree, denies, and then stores a per-resource denial. The fallback is not actually fresh for inherited or team-based permissions, so the creator-can-access fix is incomplete.

findings.title: Unbounded per-resource denial keys
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey includes resource name and parent folder, so there is one cache entry per user per action per resource, whereas permCache has one entry per user per action. Enumerating many random dashboard/folder UIDs creates unbounded denial entries that live for the full TTL, evicting useful entries and growing memory. An attacker or scanner can churn the shared local cache this way. Denial caching should be bounded or avoid per-resource negative caching.
